references.text: The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus asks the same question to the disciples, and Peter answers: "You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God." This is the most detailed version of Peter's confession.
The parallel passage in Mark where Peter confesses Jesus as the Messiah (Christ). Mark's version is the most concise: "You are the Messiah."
Peter's confession in the Gospel of John where he says: "You are the Holy One of God." Another occasion, but with a similar confession of Jesus' identity.
Martha's confession that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, which corresponds to Peter's confession in content and theological significance.
Andrew tells his brother Simon Peter that they have found the Messiah (Christ), an early confession of Jesus' messianic identity.

Simeon had received a promise from the Holy Spirit that he would not die before he had seen the Lord's Messiah (Christ). The expression "the Lord's Anointed" / "God's Christ" connects directly to Peter's confession.
The psalm speaks of the Lord's anointed (Messiah), the same expression that Peter uses for Jesus: "God's Christ" (the anointed one).
Daniel's prophecy about the Anointed One (Messiah) who is to come, the Old Testament background for Peter's confession of Jesus as Christ (Messiah).
The prophecy about the anointed one (Messiah) upon whom the Lord's Spirit rests – a key text for understanding the concept of Messiah that Peter confesses.
On Pentecost, Peter proclaims that God has made Jesus both Lord and Messiah (Christ), an elaboration of the confession he gave in Luke 9:20.
John writes that his Gospel is written so that readers may believe that Jesus is the Messiah (Christ), the Son of God – the central content of Peter's confession.

The immediate context: Jesus first asks who the crowds say he is, and the disciples report that people think he is John the Baptist, Elijah, or one of the old prophets. Then Jesus directs the question directly to the disciples in verse 20.
